title: Call an external service

  order: 6.2

import { Aside, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**Task:** call a service outside the network — a captcha check, a payment
API, a model, any HTTPS API — and write what it answers into state.

A run may ask its node for **one** HTTPS request. The node makes it only when
every gate below holds and answers with its reason otherwise. Outbound requests
are **off on every node by default**: an app that needs them runs only on nodes
whose operator turned them on, for its hosts or for any host an app declares.

## The gates

| Gate | Who sets it |
| --- | --- |
| `[context.outbound] enabled = true`, and the request's host is in `hosts` (or `hosts` holds `"*"`: any host an installed app declares) | The node's operator |
| The request's URL is under a prefix in the app's signed manifest (`outbound`): the same host, and the prefix's path or one below it at a `/`, with any query string | The app's publisher |
| The namespace the run belongs to approved a prefix that covers the URL, for the app's publisher | The namespace's admins, at install or upgrade |
| The run writes state and executes on this node, as its own write or one it relays for an author: not a view, a migration, a state op or a peer's delta | The node |
| One request per run; `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`; `https` on port 443 to a DNS name that resolves only to public addresses; no fragment; no redirect followed; no proxy | The node |
| Request body ≤ 64 KiB, URL ≤ 2 KiB, ≤ 8 headers of ≤ 1 KiB, response body ≤ 1 MiB (a longer one is refused, not cut), 10 s for the whole request | The node (`calimero_primitives::outbound`) |
| `Host`, `Cookie`, `Connection`, `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Proxy-*` and `X-Forwarded-*` headers are refused | The node |

A refusal is a reason the method can handle (`Err(String)`). A refusal by the
namespace starts with a stable word an app can match on:

- `NotApproved:` the namespace has not approved the prefix the URL is under.
  It never approved anything for this publisher, or an admin saw the prefix and
  left it out or revoked it. Tell a member to ask an admin.
- `AwaitingApproval:` a later version of the app declares the prefix and no
  admin has been asked about it yet. The prefixes approved before keep working.
  Show an admin what to approve.

`OutboundRefusal::of` reads the word for you:

```rust
use calimero_sdk::outbound::OutboundRefusal;

match env::http_request(&request) {
    Ok(response) => { /* decide, and store the decision */ }
    Err(reason) => match OutboundRefusal::of(&reason) {
        Some(OutboundRefusal::NotApproved) => { /* ask an admin of the namespace */ }
        Some(OutboundRefusal::AwaitingApproval) => { /* an admin approves the upgrade's new prefix */ }
        None => { /* anything else is a bug in the app or its deployment */ }
    },
}
```

A run with no
outbound client at all (the node's feature is off, the manifest declares
nothing, or the run is a view) and a second request in one run trap the run.

## Secrets

The app never holds a secret. A request names one as `{{secret:NAME}}` in a
header value or the body; the node fills it in from **its operator's**
secrets, for this app only (the package and signer of the installed bundle,
never anything the app says), and only into a request to a host the operator
bound that secret to. Any copy of it in the response is replaced with
`[redacted]` before the app sees the response. So a method cannot write the
secret into state, where it would replicate to every member.

<Steps>

1. Declare the URL prefixes in `Cargo.toml`. They are signed into the
   bundle's manifest and shown at install, so declare the narrowest that
   works:

   ```toml
   [package.metadata.calimero]
   outbound = [
     "https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify",
     "https://api.stripe.com/v1/",   # every path below /v1/
   ]
   ```

2. Make the request from a method that writes, and store the decision:

   ```rust
   use calimero_sdk::env;
   use calimero_sdk::outbound::{OutboundMethod, OutboundRequest};

   pub fn submit(&mut self, answer: String, captcha_token: String) -> app::Result<()> {
       let response = env::http_request(&OutboundRequest {
           method: OutboundMethod::Post,
           url: "https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify".to_owned(),
           headers: vec![(
               "Content-Type".to_owned(),
               "application/x-www-form-urlencoded".to_owned(),
           )],
           body: format!("secret={{{{secret:TURNSTILE_SECRET}}}}&response={captcha_token}")
               .into_bytes(),
       })
       .map_err(|reason| app::err!("captcha check failed: {reason}"))?;
       if response.status != 200 || !String::from_utf8_lossy(&response.body).contains(r#""success":true"#) {
           app::bail!("captcha not solved");
       }
       self.answers.push(answer.into())?;
       Ok(())
   }
   ```

3. On the node, allow the host and supply the secret (see
   [the operator's side](#the-operators-side)).

</Steps>

<Aside type="caution" title="Only the executing node asks">
The request runs once, on the node that executes the method. Peers apply the
resulting delta; they never repeat the request and never see its response.
Store the decision, not the response, and do not make a write depend on a
second node agreeing with the first.
</Aside>

## Secrets the namespace keeps, for its TEEs

An operator's secret serves one node and is set in its config. When a team
should manage the secret itself, and every TEE of the namespace should be able
to use it with nobody configuring anything, the app seals it to the
**namespace TEE key** and keeps it in its own state:

```rust
use calimero_sdk::env;
use calimero_sdk::outbound::SealedSecret;

/// Admins only. The value is in this call and never in state.
pub fn set_captcha_secret(&mut self, secret: String) -> app::Result<()> {
    let Some(sealed): Option<SealedSecret> =
        env::seal_outbound_secret(&secret, &["challenges.cloudflare.com"])
    else {
        app::bail!("this namespace has no TEE: add one before storing the secret");
    };
    self.captcha_secret.set(Some(sealed));
    Ok(())
}

// Later, in a write on any member's node:
let body = format!("secret={}&response={token}", sealed.placeholder());
```

- **Who can read it.** Every member replicates the `SealedSecret`; only a
  node that is a TEE authority of the namespace opens it, and only while it is
  one. It fills the value into the request, to one of the hosts sealed with
  it, and removes it from the response, exactly as for `{{secret:…}}`. The
  app's code holds only `{{sealed:<hex>}}`.
- **Where the request runs.** The run stays on the member's node that took
  the call, and stores what it learned there: a TEE node's own runs are
  read-only. When that node is not a TEE, it checks the request against its
  own gates and hands just that request to a TEE of the namespace over the
  sync stream, proving its context identity. The TEE serves a member of the
  context that may write there, checks every gate again under its own
  operator's policy, opens the secret, sends the request and signs the
  redacted response; the member's node takes it only under the signature of
  a TEE authority of the namespace. The method gets the answer in the same
  call, as if the request had gone out from its own node.
- **No TEE, no secret.** `env::seal_outbound_secret` answers `None` while the
  namespace has no TEE key (`env::tee_sealing_key`), so the app can tell the
  admin to add a TEE first. A request naming a sealed secret is refused with
  `SealedUnavailable:` (`OutboundRefusal::SealedUnavailable`) when no TEE of
  the namespace can be reached.
- **New TEEs.** A TEE admitted later is handed the namespace key by one that
  holds it, and opens what was sealed before it joined.
- **Rotation.** When a TEE stops being an authority, the namespace key
  rotates, and `env::tee_sealing_key` names the new one. Have an admin set the
  secret again; compare `SealedSecret::key` with `env::tee_sealing_key` to tell
  them. Until then the TEEs that remain still open the old envelope, and so
  does the TEE that left.
- **The operator's part** stays: outbound requests on, and the host allowed,
  on the TEE nodes, and on the member's node that takes the call, whose gates
  are checked first. No secret to configure.

## The namespace's side

The namespace's data is what a run can send, so the namespace agrees to the
hosts too: the operator allowing a host and the publisher declaring it are not
enough. An admin (or a member holding `MANAGE_APPLICATION`, who may also set
the namespace's application) approves in the call that installs or upgrades
the app, so the install screen lists the hosts in the confirm the admin
already clicks:

```json
POST /admin-api/namespaces
{ "applicationId": "…", "approveOutbound": "manifest" }

POST /admin-api/groups/{groupId}/upgrade
{ "targetApplicationId": "…", "approveOutbound": ["https://api.stripe.com/v1/"] }
```

`"manifest"` approves every prefix the app declares; a list approves those.
Leave the field out and the app's requests answer `NotApproved` until an
admin approves. An app that declares no `outbound` needs and publishes nothing.

- **Once per namespace.** The approval is published at the namespace root as
  a `GroupOp::OutboundApprovalSet` and every subgroup and context reads it.
- **Per publisher.** It is keyed by the bundle's signer, so a fork or a
  transferred app signed by someone else starts with nothing approved.
- **Upgrades only add.** An upgrade's approval is added to what the namespace
  approves. A prefix the new version declares that nobody approved waits
  (`AwaitingApproval`); the rest keep working.
- **Revoke by setting the list.** `PUT /admin-api/namespaces/{id}/outbound-approvals`
  with `{ "applicationId": "…", "approve": [ … ] }` sets the publisher's list
  exactly, and an empty list revokes everything. It takes effect at the next
  run. `GET` on the same path lists what the namespace approves, per publisher.

With `meroctl`: `namespace create --approve-outbound manifest`,
`group upgrade trigger --approve-outbound <prefixes>`, and
`namespace outbound ls|set`.

## The operator's side

`[context.outbound]` in the node's `config.toml`:

```toml
[context.outbound]
enabled = true
hosts = ["challenges.cloudflare.com", "api.stripe.com"]   # or ["*"]

# Secrets from environment variables, read once at start: a missing one
# fails the start.
[context.outbound.env_secrets.TURNSTILE_SECRET]
env = "MERO_TURNSTILE_SECRET"
packages = ["com.calimero.mero-forms"]
signers = ["did:key:z6Mk…"]   # the bundle's signerId
hosts = ["challenges.cloudflare.com"]
```

`hosts = ["*"]` lets every installed app reach the hosts its own signed
manifest declares and its namespace approved, so a new app needs no config
change. Every other gate still holds, and a secret still goes only to the hosts
bound to it.

Instead of `env_secrets`, a node can ask a secrets service beside it
(exclusive with `env_secrets`):

```toml
[context.outbound.sidecar]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:7070/v1/secret"
token_env = "MERO_SECRETS_TOKEN"
```

The node `POST`s `{"package", "signer", "name"}` with the token as a bearer and
expects `200 {"value", "hosts"}` or `404`. The URL must be `http` on a loopback
address. A managed deployment answers there with the secrets a deployer set
for their app, for every namespace that runs it, so the secret lives on the
nodes that serve the app and nowhere else.

The node logs every request it makes or refuses, with the context, the app
and the URL, never the secret.

A secret is matched on both the package and the bundle's signer: anyone can
name a package, only its publisher can sign it.

## Test it

`env::http_request` needs a node: under `TestHost` it returns
`Err("outbound requests need a node")`, so unit-test the logic around the
answer by passing the answer in.

End to end, run a cluster scenario: the scenario runner's nodes are the test
build of the node (`outbound-testing`), whose settings accept a
testing table that a release build refuses. A scenario gives its nodes that
TOML as `cluster.settings`:

```toml
[context.outbound]
enabled = true
hosts = ["echo.outbound.test"]

[context.outbound.testing]
echo = true          # .test hosts are answered in-process

[context.outbound.testing.secrets.ECHO_KEY]
value = "s3cr3t-e2e" # a literal, so the test needs no environment
packages = ["com.calimero.outbound-probe"]
signers = ["did:key:z6Mk…"]
hosts = ["echo.outbound.test"]
```

The echo answers `200` with the request the node sent, as JSON: method, URL,
path, query, headers, body and the number of secrets filled in. It answers only
after every gate has passed, and its answer is redacted like any other, so a
scenario sees exactly what left the node. `apps/outbound-probe` and its
scenarios (`scenarios/cluster/outbound.json`, and `outbound-off.json` for a
cluster with outbound off) cover every gate this way:

```bash
cargo test -p calimero-node --test scenarios -- outbound-probe
```

## Where it stops

- A request never runs in a view. Read the answer back from state.
- Members who run the app on their own node need outbound requests on
  there too, or their writes that call `http_request` trap. Route those writes
  to a node that has them (a relay or a TEE).
- Redaction removes the secret as sent. A service that answers with it
  encoded (base64, URL-escaped) defeats it, so bind a secret only to hosts that
  do not echo it.
- The response is not authenticated beyond TLS: a service you call can answer
  anything, so call only services you trust for the decision you store.
